title: Haematology I: Blood Cells and Anaemias
description: Haematopoiesis, the full blood count and blood film, red cell indices, classification and laboratory diagnosis of anaemias, and haemoglobinopathies.

topics.title: Haematopoiesis and Blood Cell Morphology
topics.summary: Sites of blood formation, cell lineages, growth factors and normal cell morphology.

notes.b: Blood formation occurs in the yolk sac (first weeks of embryonic life), then the liver and spleen (fetal period), and the bone marrow from about the 7th month of gestation onward; in adults active marrow is mainly in the axial skeleton (vertebrae, pelvis, sternum, ribs, skull) and proximal femur and humerus. Pluripotent haematopoietic stem cells (CD34+) give rise to myeloid progenitors (erythrocytes, granulocytes, monocytes, megakaryocytes) and lymphoid progenitors. Growth factors: erythropoietin (red cells), thrombopoietin (platelets), G-CSF (neutrophils), GM-CSF. Extramedullary haematopoiesis in the liver and spleen occurs in severe chronic anaemias and marrow infiltration.
k: Sites: yolk sac → liver/spleen → bone marrow
EPO: red cells; TPO: platelets; G-CSF: neutrophils

notes.b: Red cell maturation: proerythroblast → basophilic, polychromatic and orthochromatic erythroblasts → reticulocyte → mature red cell (about 7 days). Reticulocytes contain residual RNA, stained supravitally with new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue; a normal count is about 0.5–2.5%. The reticulocyte count distinguishes marrow underproduction (low) from haemolysis or bleeding (high). Normal red cells are biconcave discs about 7–8 µm with central pallor; a Romanowsky stain (Leishman, Giemsa, Wright) is used for blood films. Abnormal forms: target cells (HbC, thalassaemia, liver disease), sickle cells, spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis, autoimmune haemolysis), schistocytes/fragments (DIC, microangiopathy), tear drops (myelofibrosis), pencil cells (iron deficiency).

q: In adults, active haematopoiesis occurs mainly in the:
Bone marrow of the axial skeleton
Adults use marrow in vertebrae, pelvis, sternum and ribs.

Erythropoietin from the kidney drives erythropoiesis.
A raised reticulocyte count in an anaemic patient suggests:
The marrow responds to red cell loss.

The stain routinely used for blood films in Nigerian laboratories is:

Tear-drop red cells are characteristic of:

Haematopoiesis in the fetus from about the 7th month occurs mainly in the:

topics.title: Full Blood Count and Red Cell Indices
topics.summary: Components of the FBC, calculation and interpretation of indices, and ESR.

notes.b: The full blood count reports haemoglobin (Hb), packed cell volume (PCV/haematocrit), red cell count (RBC), red cell indices, white cell count with differential, and platelets. Indices: mean cell volume MCV = PCV / RBC (normal 80–100 fL); mean cell haemoglobin MCH = Hb / RBC (27–32 pg); mean cell haemoglobin concentration MCHC = Hb / PCV (32–36 g/dL); red cell distribution width (RDW) reflects variation in size (anisocytosis) and rises early in iron deficiency. Manual methods: Hb by the cyanmethaemoglobin (Drabkin's) method, PCV by microhaematocrit centrifugation, counts with a haemocytometer (Neubauer chamber). Automated analysers use impedance (Coulter principle) and flow cytometry.

The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (Westergren method, 1 hour) rises with increased plasma fibrinogen and globulins (inflammation, infection, TB, myeloma, pregnancy) and anaemia; it is non-specific. MCV classifies anaemia: microcytic (< 80 fL — iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic anaemia, lead), normocytic (acute blood loss, chronic disease, renal failure, haemolysis, marrow failure) and macrocytic (> 100 fL — B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, drugs such as hydroxyurea and zidovudine).

q: The normal range for MCV in adults is about:
It is the haemoglobin concentration in packed red cells.
An anaemia with MCV 68 fL is most likely due to:
Iron deficiency is the commonest microcytic anaemia.

It measures all haemoglobin forms except sulfhaemoglobin.

Hydroxyurea impairs DNA synthesis, raising MCV.

topics.title: Iron Deficiency and Megaloblastic Anaemias
topics.summary: Iron metabolism, iron studies, vitamin B12 and folate deficiency and their laboratory diagnosis.

notes.b: Iron is absorbed in the duodenum as Fe2+ via DMT1, stored as ferritin and transported by transferrin; hepcidin from the liver regulates absorption and release. Causes of iron deficiency in Nigeria: chronic blood loss (hookworm, menorrhagia, gastrointestinal bleeding), increased requirements (pregnancy, infancy, adolescence) and poor intake. Laboratory features: microcytic hypochromic cells, pencil cells, raised RDW, low serum ferritin (the best single test — but ferritin rises in inflammation), low serum iron, raised total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) and low transferrin saturation, absent bone-marrow iron stores (Perls' Prussian blue stain). In anaemia of chronic disease, ferritin is normal or raised with low TIBC.
k: Ferritin: best single test for iron stores
Hookworm is a major Nigerian cause

notes.b: Deficiency of vitamin B12 or folate impairs DNA synthesis, causing megaloblastic changes: macrocytic oval red cells (MCV often > 110 fL), hypersegmented neutrophils (≥ 6 lobes — an early sign), pancytopenia, raised LDH and bilirubin (ineffective erythropoiesis) and megaloblastic marrow. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes are pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor — anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies), gastrectomy, ileal disease, strict vegan diet and fish tapeworm; it also causes neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration). Folate deficiency results from poor diet, pregnancy, haemolysis (sickle cell disease), malabsorption, alcohol and drugs (methotrexate, phenytoin, trimethoprim). Giving folate alone to a B12-deficient patient may worsen neurological damage.
k: Don't give folate alone in B12 deficiency

q: The best single test to assess body iron stores is:

topics.title: Haemolytic Anaemias
topics.summary: Mechanisms and laboratory features of haemolysis, hereditary and acquired causes.

notes.b: Haemolysis is premature red cell destruction. Laboratory evidence: anaemia with raised reticulocyte count (polychromasia), raised unconjugated bilirubin, raised LDH, reduced haptoglobin, and urinary urobilinogen; intravascular haemolysis also causes haemoglobinaemia, haemoglobinuria and haemosiderinuria. The direct antiglobulin test (DAT, direct Coombs') detects antibody or complement on red cells — positive in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, haemolytic transfusion reactions and haemolytic disease of the newborn.

Hereditary: membrane defects (hereditary spherocytosis — spherocytes, raised MCHC, increased osmotic fragility, negative DAT; treated with splenectomy in severe cases), enzyme defects (G6PD deficiency — episodic haemolysis with oxidant drugs, infections or fava beans; Heinz bodies and 'bite cells'; G6PD assay should be repeated after the acute episode because reticulocytes have higher enzyme levels; pyruvate kinase deficiency) and haemoglobinopathies (sickle cell disease, thalassaemias). Acquired: immune (warm IgG autoimmune — e.g. SLE, lymphoma, drugs; cold IgM — Mycoplasma, EBV), malaria (a leading cause in Nigeria), microangiopathic (DIC, HUS, TTP), mechanical heart valves, snake envenoming and burns.
k: G6PD: Heinz bodies, bite cells; retest later
Malaria is a major cause of haemolysis

topics.title: Haemoglobinopathies and Their Laboratory Diagnosis
topics.summary: Sickle cell disease, HbC and thalassaemias; electrophoresis, HPLC and screening tests.

notes.b: HbS results from a Glu→Val substitution at position 6 of the β-globin chain; deoxygenated HbS polymerises, deforming cells into sickles, causing vaso-occlusion and haemolysis. HbSS disease: chronic haemolytic anaemia (Hb often 6–9 g/dL), vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic sequestration and auto-splenectomy (Howell–Jolly bodies), infections, aplastic crises (parvovirus B19). HbC (Glu→Lys at β6) forms crystals and target cells; HbSC disease is milder but has more retinopathy and avascular necrosis. The sickling (sodium metabisulphite) and solubility tests detect HbS but do not distinguish AS from SS — haemoglobin electrophoresis (cellulose acetate at alkaline pH: order from anode A > F > S > C) or HPLC is needed.
k: HbS: Glu→Val β6; HbC: Glu→Lys β6
Sickling test can't distinguish AS from SS

notes.b: Thalassaemias are reduced synthesis of globin chains. β-thalassaemia trait (minor): mild microcytic anaemia with low MCV disproportionate to Hb, raised red cell count, target cells and raised HbA2 (> 3.5%) — distinguish from iron deficiency (normal ferritin; Mentzer index MCV/RBC < 13 favours thalassaemia). β-thalassaemia major presents at 6–12 months with severe anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly and skull bossing ('hair-on-end' X-ray); it requires regular transfusion and iron chelation. α-thalassaemia results from deletion of α-globin genes (four genes): silent carrier (1 deleted), trait (2), HbH disease (3), Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis (4 — incompatible with life).
